blocks.body:
The region under $y = 1/x^2$ to the right of $x = 1$ is infinitely long. Does it have a finite area? The integral from $1$ to $b$ is $1 - \frac1b$, which approaches $1$ as $b$ grows, so it is natural to say the area is $1$. The same computation for $y = 1/x$ gives $\ln b$, which grows without bound: that region has infinite area, even though $1/x$ also tends to $0$.

The [[riemann-integral|definite integral]] only makes sense for bounded functions on bounded intervals. Improper integrals extend it by taking limits, and the interesting questions are when the limit exists and how to tell without computing it. Many of the integrals that matter most, like $\int_0^\infty x^{s-1}e^{-x}\,dx$ or $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-x^2}\,dx$, are of this kind.

blocks.title: Improper integral
blocks.body:
Suppose $f$ is integrable on $[a, b]$ for every $b > a$. If the limit
$$\int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx = \lim_{b \to \infty} \int_a^b f(x)\,dx$$
exists and is finite, the improper integral converges and has this value; otherwise it diverges. Likewise, if $f$ is integrable on $[c, b]$ for every $c \in (a, b)$ but possibly unbounded near $a$, then $\int_a^b f = \lim_{c \to a^+} \int_c^b f$. An integral over $(-\infty, \infty)$, or one with trouble at both ends, is split at an interior point, and it converges only if both pieces converge.

In words: integrate over a region where nothing goes wrong, then let the region grow to the whole thing.

blocks.title: The p-test and some first examples
blocks.body:
For $p \ne 1$ and $b > 1$,
$$\int_1^b \frac{dx}{x^p} = \frac{1 - b^{1-p}}{p - 1}.$$
If $p > 1$, then $b^{1-p} \to 0$ and the integral converges to $\frac{1}{p-1}$; if $p < 1$, then $b^{1-p} \to \infty$. For $p = 1$ the integral is $\ln b \to \infty$. So $\int_1^\infty x^{-p}\,dx$ converges exactly when $p > 1$. Near $0$ the roles are reversed: $\int_c^1 x^{-p}\,dx = \frac{1 - c^{1-p}}{1-p}$ for $p \ne 1$, which converges as $c \to 0^+$ exactly when $p < 1$, to $\frac{1}{1-p}$. For example $\int_0^1 \frac{dx}{\sqrt x} = 2$ although the integrand is unbounded.

A small table makes the difference between $p = 2$ and $p = 1$ concrete:
$$\begin{array}{c|cccc} b & 10 & 100 & 1000 & 10^6 \\ \hline \int_1^b x^{-2}\,dx & 0.9 & 0.99 & 0.999 & 0.999999 \\ \int_1^b x^{-1}\,dx & 2.30 & 4.61 & 6.91 & 13.8 \end{array}$$
The second row grows slowly, but it does grow past every bound.

Exponentials decay faster than any power, so integrals like $\int_0^\infty x^n e^{-x}\,dx$ converge. Logarithms are milder than any power: $\int_0^1 \ln x\,dx = \lim_{c\to 0^+}\big[x\ln x - x\big]_c^1 = -1$, since $c \ln c \to 0$.

blocks.title: Comparison tests
blocks.body:
Let $f$ and $g$ be integrable on every interval $[a, b]$ with $b > a$.

1. If $0 \le f(x) \le g(x)$ for all $x \ge a$ and $\int_a^\infty g$ converges, then $\int_a^\infty f$ converges and $\int_a^\infty f \le \int_a^\infty g$. Equivalently, if $\int_a^\infty f$ diverges, so does $\int_a^\infty g$.
2. If $f(x) > 0$, $g(x) > 0$ and $f(x)/g(x) \to L$ with $0 < L < \infty$ as $x \to \infty$, then $\int_a^\infty f$ and $\int_a^\infty g$ either both converge or both diverge.

The same statements hold for integrals that are improper at a finite endpoint.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
1. Put $F(b) = \int_a^b f$ and $G(b) = \int_a^b g$. Because $f, g \ge 0$, both are nondecreasing in $b$, and $F(b) \le G(b) \le M$, where $M = \lim G = \int_a^\infty g$. So $F$ is nondecreasing and bounded above. Let $S = \sup_{b > a} F(b)$, which exists by the completeness of the [[real-numbers]]. Given $\varepsilon > 0$, there is $b_0$ with $F(b_0) > S - \varepsilon$, and then $S - \varepsilon < F(b) \le S$ for all $b \ge b_0$. Hence $F(b) \to S \le M$.

2. Since $f/g \to L$, there is $X \ge a$ with $\frac{L}{2} g(x) \le f(x) \le 2L\,g(x)$ for $x \ge X$. Convergence of $\int_a^\infty$ is the same as convergence of $\int_X^\infty$, because $\int_a^X$ is an ordinary finite integral. If $\int_X^\infty g$ converges, then so does $\int_X^\infty 2Lg$, and part 1 gives convergence of $\int_X^\infty f$. If $\int_X^\infty f$ converges, apply part 1 to $\frac{L}{2} g \le f$.

blocks.title: Absolute and conditional convergence
blocks.body:
For integrands that change sign, the comparison test applies to $|f|$. We say $\int_a^\infty f$ converges absolutely if $\int_a^\infty |f|$ converges. Absolute convergence implies convergence: since $0 \le f + |f| \le 2|f|$, the integral of $f + |f|$ converges by comparison, and $f = (f + |f|) - |f|$ is a difference of two convergent integrals. For example $\int_1^\infty \frac{\cos x}{x^2}\,dx$ converges absolutely because $\left|\frac{\cos x}{x^2}\right| \le \frac{1}{x^2}$.

The famous example of an integral that converges but not absolutely is $\int_1^\infty \frac{\sin x}{x}\,dx$. Integrating by parts on $[1, b]$,
$$\int_1^b \frac{\sin x}{x}\,dx = \cos 1 - \frac{\cos b}{b} - \int_1^b \frac{\cos x}{x^2}\,dx.$$
As $b \to \infty$, the middle term tends to $0$ and the last integral converges absolutely, so the left side has a limit. The cancellation between positive and negative humps is essential, because the humps alone are too big: on $[k\pi, (k+1)\pi]$ we have $\frac1x \ge \frac{1}{(k+1)\pi}$ and $\int_{k\pi}^{(k+1)\pi} |\sin x|\,dx = 2$, so
$$\int_{\pi}^{(N+1)\pi} \frac{|\sin x|}{x}\,dx \ \ge\ \frac{2}{\pi}\sum_{k=1}^{N} \frac{1}{k+1} \to \infty.$$
(The value $\int_0^\infty \frac{\sin x}{x}\,dx = \frac{\pi}{2}$ is a classical result; it is not obtainable from an elementary antiderivative.)

blocks.title: Integral test
blocks.body:
Let $f$ be positive and nonincreasing on $[1, \infty)$. Then $\sum_{n=1}^\infty f(n)$ converges if and only if $\int_1^\infty f(x)\,dx$ converges. Moreover, for every $N \ge 2$,
$$\sum_{n=2}^{N} f(n) \ \le\ \int_1^N f(x)\,dx \ \le\ \sum_{n=1}^{N-1} f(n).$$

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body: A monotone function is integrable on every bounded interval. For $k \le x \le k + 1$ we have $f(k+1) \le f(x) \le f(k)$, so integrating over $[k, k+1]$ gives $f(k+1) \le \int_k^{k+1} f \le f(k)$. Summing over $k = 1, \dots, N-1$ gives the displayed inequality. Both the partial sums and $\int_1^b f$ are nondecreasing (in $N$ and in $b$), so each converges if and only if it is bounded. The left inequality shows that a bounded integral gives bounded partial sums, and the right inequality shows the converse; for non-integer $b$ use $\int_1^b f \le \int_1^{\lceil b \rceil} f$.

blocks.title: Moments of the exponential
blocks.body: Show that $\displaystyle\int_0^\infty x^n e^{-x}\,dx = n!$ for every integer $n \ge 0$.
blocks.solution:
For $n = 0$: $\int_0^b e^{-x}\,dx = 1 - e^{-b} \to 1 = 0!$. For $n \ge 1$, integrate by parts on $[0, b]$ with $u = x^n$, $v = -e^{-x}$:
$$\int_0^b x^n e^{-x}\,dx = -b^n e^{-b} + n\int_0^b x^{n-1} e^{-x}\,dx.$$
Since $b^n e^{-b} \to 0$ as $b \to \infty$ (for instance by applying [[lhopital|L'Hôpital's rule]] $n$ times), letting $b \to \infty$ gives $J_n = n J_{n-1}$, where $J_n$ denotes the integral; the right side converges by induction, so the left side does too. With $J_0 = 1$, induction gives $J_n = n!$. Replacing $n$ by a real number $s - 1$ with $s > 0$ defines the [[gamma]] function, $\Gamma(s) = \int_0^\infty x^{s-1} e^{-x}\,dx$, which extends the factorial.

blocks.title: Trouble at both ends
blocks.body: Decide whether $\displaystyle\int_0^\infty \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x}\,(1 + x)}$ converges, and if so find its value.
blocks.solution:
The integrand is unbounded at $0$ and the interval is unbounded, so split at $1$. Near $0$ the integrand is comparable to $x^{-1/2}$ (their ratio tends to $1$), and $\int_0^1 x^{-1/2}\,dx$ converges since $\frac12 < 1$. Near infinity it is comparable to $x^{-3/2}$, and $\int_1^\infty x^{-3/2}\,dx$ converges since $\frac32 > 1$. By the limit comparison test, both pieces converge.

To compute it, substitute $x = t^2$, $dx = 2t\,dt$ on $[c, b]$ and then let $c \to 0^+$, $b \to \infty$:
$$\int_{\sqrt c}^{\sqrt b} \frac{2t\,dt}{t(1 + t^2)} = 2\big(\arctan \sqrt b - \arctan \sqrt c\big) \to 2\cdot\frac{\pi}{2} = \pi.$$

blocks.title: A borderline family of series
blocks.body: For which real $p$ does $\displaystyle\sum_{n=2}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n(\ln n)^p}$ converge?
blocks.solution:
For $p \le 0$ the terms are at least $\frac1n$ once $n \ge 3$ (then $\ln n > 1$), and the series diverges by comparison with the harmonic series. For $p > 0$ the function $f(x) = \frac{1}{x(\ln x)^p}$ is positive and decreasing on $[2, \infty)$, so the integral test applies (starting at $2$ instead of $1$ changes nothing in the proof). With $u = \ln x$, $du = dx/x$,
$$\int_2^b \frac{dx}{x(\ln x)^p} = \int_{\ln 2}^{\ln b} \frac{du}{u^p},$$
and by the $p$-test this has a finite limit as $b \to \infty$ exactly when $p > 1$. So the series converges if and only if $p > 1$. For $p = 1$ the integral bound shows that the partial sums up to $N$ are at most $\ln\ln N + 1.1$: they diverge, but $N$ needs more than $3000$ digits before the sum passes $10$. This is the sort of slow divergence that appears with sums over primes, such as $\sum_p \frac1p$.

blocks.title: A logarithmic integral by symmetry
blocks.body: Show that $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} \ln(\sin x)\,dx$ converges and equals $-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\ln 2$.
blocks.solution:
Convergence. On $(0, \frac{\pi}{2}]$ we have $\frac{2x}{\pi} \le \sin x \le 1$ (the graph of $\sin$ is concave there, so it lies above the chord from $(0,0)$ to $(\frac{\pi}{2}, 1)$). Hence $0 \le -\ln \sin x \le -\ln\frac{2x}{\pi}$, and $\int_0^{\pi/2} -\ln\frac{2x}{\pi}\,dx$ converges because $\int_0^1 \ln x\,dx = -1$ does. By comparison, $I = \int_0^{\pi/2} \ln \sin x\,dx$ converges.

Value. The substitution $x \mapsto \frac{\pi}{2} - x$ shows $I = \int_0^{\pi/2} \ln \cos x\,dx$. Adding the two forms and using $\sin x \cos x = \frac12 \sin 2x$,
$$2I = \int_0^{\pi/2} \ln\Big(\frac{\sin 2x}{2}\Big)\,dx = -\frac{\pi}{2}\ln 2 + \int_0^{\pi/2} \ln \sin 2x\,dx.$$
With $t = 2x$ the last integral is $\frac12\int_0^{\pi} \ln \sin t\,dt$. Since $\sin(\pi - t) = \sin t$, the integral over $[0, \pi]$ is twice the integral over $[0, \frac{\pi}{2}]$, so the last term equals $\frac12 \cdot 2I = I$. Therefore $2I = -\frac{\pi}{2}\ln 2 + I$, and $I = -\frac{\pi}{2} \ln 2$. Every manipulation here is legitimate because all the integrals involved converge; with divergent integrals, the same algebra could produce nonsense.

blocks.body:
- Not noticing that an integral is improper. $\int_{-1}^{1} \frac{dx}{x^2}$ is not $\big[-\frac1x\big]_{-1}^{1} = -2$: the integrand is unbounded at $0$ and the integral diverges.
- Taking symmetric limits. $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x\,dx$ diverges even though $\int_{-R}^{R} x\,dx = 0$ for every $R$; both halves must converge separately. (The symmetric limit is called the Cauchy principal value, a different notion.)
- Thinking $f(x) \to 0$ is enough. $\frac1x \to 0$, but $\int_1^\infty \frac{dx}{x}$ diverges.
- Thinking $f(x) \to 0$ is necessary. Unlike the terms of a convergent series, the integrand of a convergent integral need not tend to $0$: $\int_0^\infty \sin(x^2)\,dx$ converges (substitute $u = x^2$ and argue as for $\frac{\sin u}{\sqrt u}$), although $\sin(x^2)$ keeps oscillating between $-1$ and $1$.
- Using comparison for functions of changing sign. The comparison test needs $0 \le f \le g$; for other functions compare $|f|$, and remember that this tests absolute convergence only.

The [[gamma]] function $\Gamma(s) = \int_0^\infty x^{s-1}e^{-x}\,dx$ converges for $s > 0$ by exactly the arguments above (compare with $x^{s-1}$ near $0$ and with $x^{-2}$ near infinity). The integral test links integrals with [[series]], and its refinement, Euler–Maclaurin summation in [[partial-summation]], estimates sums such as $\sum_{n \le N} \frac1n = \ln N + \gamma + o(1)$, where $\gamma \approx 0.5772$ is Euler's constant.

Continuous probability [[distributions]] are densities whose improper integral over $\mathbb R$ is $1$; the normal density relies on $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-x^2}\,dx = \sqrt\pi$, which is computed in [[multiple-integrals]]. Fourier transforms ([[fourier-poisson]]) and the [[mellin]] transform are improper integrals depending on a parameter, and the [[zeta]] function has the representation $\Gamma(s)\zeta(s) = \int_0^\infty \frac{x^{s-1}}{e^x - 1}\,dx$ for $s > 1$. In the theory of the [[lebesgue]] integral, absolutely convergent improper integrals are integrable, while $\int_0^\infty \frac{\sin x}{x}\,dx$ exists only as a limit.

2. For $a > 0$, compute $\int_0^\infty e^{-ax}\cos x\,dx$.
3. Show that $\int_0^\infty \frac{\sin^2 x}{x^2}\,dx$ converges.
4. Does $\sum_{n \ge 3} \frac{1}{n \ln n \,\ln\ln n}$ converge?
